lessons.lesson:
This month you build **Triage**: a small issue board for a team, where issues move from Open to In progress to Done. Before any of that you need four tools, and you need to know what each one is for.

### One tool, one job
- **VS Code** is where you read and edit files. It has a terminal built in, so you rarely need another window.
- **Node.js** runs JavaScript on your machine, outside a browser. It brings **npm** with it, for installing packages other people wrote.
- **Git** records the history of your files, so you can go back, compare, and work on a branch without breaking what works.
- **GitHub** is a website that hosts that history, so your mentor can see it and comment on it.

### Install in that order
For Node.js choose the **LTS** release: long-term support, the version teams run in production. After installing anything, **open a new terminal before you test it**. The old terminal does not know about programs installed after it opened.

### Not on the list: Claude Code
On purpose. You install it in Week 2, when you know enough to judge what it does. Until then every lesson is done with your own hands, and that is the point.

### One rule starts today
Never paste a password, token, or key into a file in your project, a chat, or the question log. If something asks for one and you are not sure, stop and ask.

lessons.lesson:
### A program is a text file
A program is a text file that a **runtime** reads from top to bottom. For JavaScript that runtime is **Node.js**. Nothing happens to the file until you ask Node to run it, and nothing about editing it is special: a `.js` file is plain text, and VS Code is a text editor with good habits.

### The terminal stands in one folder
The terminal is a text interface to the same computer. It always stands in one folder, the **working directory**, and every command runs there.
- `pwd` prints where you are.
- `ls` lists what is here.
- `cd` moves you.

Developers type commands because they are exact and repeatable: you can see what ran, copy it, and run it again tomorrow. A double-click cannot do that.

### Read the error before you touch anything
When a program fails, Node prints an error with a **file name, a line number, and a message**. Read it from the top before changing anything. The line number is usually right and the message is usually honest. Reading an error calmly is the first developer habit, and it is worth more than any tool.

### Three habits for this month
1. Make one small change, run it, look.
2. Name things for what they are.
3. When you are stuck for twenty minutes, ask, with what you tried and what you saw.

lessons.lesson:
### Three programs talking
A web app is several programs that talk to each other.
- The **frontend** runs in the browser: it draws the board, reacts to clicks, and sends requests.
- The **backend** runs on a server: it receives those requests, checks the rules, and decides what happens.
- The **database** stores the data on disk so it survives restarts. Nobody edits it by hand; the backend does it on the frontend's behalf.

### The conversation has a fixed shape
The browser sends a **request**: a method such as `GET` or `POST`, a path such as `/api/issues`, and sometimes a body in **JSON**. The server replies with a **response**: a status code and a body.
- `200` and `201`: it worked.
- `400`: the request was wrong.
- `404`: nothing is there.
- `500`: the server broke.

The set of paths a server agrees to answer is its **API**.

### Try it
Press Add in the request tracer below and step through the six hops. That is the whole shape of Triage. In Week 2 you build the server and database hops; in Week 3 the browser hops. Every later lesson is one of these boxes, so name them now.

The server you will build is a Node.js program that listens on a port and answers these requests. The learning app you are using right now works exactly this way, which is why you will inspect it next.

lessons.summary: What a framework is, the common choices per layer, and why Triage uses React, Express, and SQLite.

lessons.lesson:
### Four words, kept simple
- A **language** is the grammar you write in: JavaScript, Python.
- A **runtime** is the program that runs that language on a machine. **Node.js** runs JavaScript outside the browser; Python's interpreter runs Python.
- A **library** is a box of ready-made functions you call when you want them. You stay in charge.
- A **framework** is the other way round: it owns the structure and calls your code at the right moments. You fill in the parts.

So **Node.js is a runtime, not a framework**. Express is a framework that runs on Node.js. React is a library, though people often say framework, and that is fine as long as you know who calls whom.

### A stack is one choice per layer
- **Frontend:** React, Vue, and Angular all build interfaces from components. React is the most used and the best documented.
- **Backend:** Express is a small Node.js framework; FastAPI and Flask are small Python ones; Django is a large Python one with everything included. **Streamlit** is different: it turns a Python script into a web page in minutes, perfect for a quick data or AI demo and wrong for a product with users and rules.
- **Database:** two families, below.

### SQL and NoSQL
**SQL** databases such as SQLite and PostgreSQL store rows in tables with fixed columns and answer questions written in SQL. They are the default when your data has a clear shape, like issues with a title and a status. **NoSQL** databases such as MongoDB store flexible documents, which suits data whose shape changes often or is very large. Triage's issues have a fixed shape, so Triage uses SQL.

### Why Triage uses React, Express, and SQLite
One language across both halves means fewer things to learn at once. Express is small enough to read in full. SQLite needs no server to install. Explore the stack map below; you do not need to remember every card, only the shape of the choice. If you already know Python, keep it: the ideas transfer directly.

lessons.lesson:
### A commit is a snapshot
Git records snapshots of your folder. Each snapshot is a **commit**: the exact state of every tracked file, plus a message saying what changed and why. Commits form a chain, so you can see what changed between any two and return to any of them. The **repository** is the folder plus that history, stored in a hidden `.git` folder.

### Commit is local, push is sharing
A commit lives on your machine until you **push** it. **GitHub** is one place to push to: it hosts the repository so your mentor can read your commits, comment, and later review a pull request. Both are needed.

### Branches keep main safe
A **branch** is a separate line of commits. `main` holds the version that works; a branch holds work in progress. You will never commit to `main` directly in this program, because a branch can be reviewed before it is merged.

`.gitignore` lists files Git must not record: `node_modules`, `.env`, database files. Secrets never enter history, because **history is forever**.

### HTTPS or SSH
Your machine talks to GitHub in one of two ways.
- **HTTPS** uses a URL starting with `https://` and asks for a token when you push.
- **SSH** uses a URL starting with `git@github.com:` and proves who you are with a key pair stored on your machine, so you never type a password or token again.

SSH is the recommended setup for this program: set it up once with GitHub's guide, test it with `ssh -T git@github.com`, and every push after that just works.

### Messages say the outcome
'Print three issue titles', not 'update file'. In the Git playground below, run each command and watch the history grow on your machine, and then on GitHub.

lessons.lesson:
### It predicts the next token
A **large language model** is a program that predicts the next piece of text. It was trained by reading an enormous amount of writing and adjusting billions of numbers until its guesses matched what came next. After training, the numbers are frozen. When you type, your text is cut into **tokens**, small chunks of a few characters, and the model predicts likely next tokens one at a time. **The answer is generated, not looked up.**

### Why it is fluent, and why it is wrong
It is fluent because fluency is what it learned. It can be **confidently wrong** because it predicts plausible text, not checked facts; nothing stops a likely-sounding sentence from being false. It also knows nothing you did not give it: the text it can see at once is its **context window**, measured in tokens, and anything outside that window does not exist for it.

### Three terms for the month
- **Machine learning** is the broad idea of programs that learn patterns from data. A spam filter is machine learning.
- **Generative AI** is the part that produces new content: text, images, code.
- A **language model** is one kind of generative AI.

Training a model takes months and millions. Writing a prompt takes a minute and changes nothing inside the model, only what it sees.

lessons.lesson:
### A model in a loop
A chat model takes text in and gives text out. An **agent** is that same model placed inside a loop with tools:
1. **Read** something: a file, an error, an output.
2. **Decide** what to do next.
3. **Act**: edit a file or run a command.
4. **Observe** the result, and decide again.

The loop runs until the task is done, or until it reaches a step that needs a human.

### Tools are how it acts
The model cannot touch your disk. It can only write a request such as 'run `node hello.js`', and a program around it runs the command and hands back the output. That is **tool use**. **Retrieval** is the same idea for knowledge: when the model needs a document, a tool fetches the relevant text and puts it in the context window, so it answers from what it was just shown rather than from memory.

### Same loop, different clothes
Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex are all this loop. **Claude Code** is the one you will use: it reads your files, proposes edits as diffs, runs commands with your permission, and **stops to ask** before anything destructive or unfamiliar. The permission prompt is not a nuisance; it is the place where you remain the decider.

### Two habits
- **Read what the agent read.** If it decided from a file you have not looked at, look.
- **Treat every edit as a proposal.** The diff is yours to accept or reject.

Next lesson you install the tool and make that real.

lessons.lesson:
### Two forms, one agent
Claude Code is the agent from the last lesson, installed on your machine. It comes in two forms that are the same program underneath:
- a **command-line tool** you start by typing `claude` in a project folder;
- a **VS Code extension** that shows the same session beside your files, with diffs you can click through.

Use whichever you like. Most people use the extension for reading diffs and the terminal for quick questions.

### Signing in
It signs in with **your own Claude.ai account**. You do not need an API key, and you must not buy anything: if sign-in fails, write to your mentor through the question log. Never paste a key or password into a session.

### Four rules from the first session
1. **Start a new session for each new task**, so old context does not leak into new work.
2. **Read every diff before accepting it.** The agent proposes; you decide.
3. **Allow only commands you understand.** The permission prompt is yours.
4. **Plan mode first** for anything touching more than one file: read the plan, then approve.

### CLAUDE.md
`CLAUDE.md` is a file in your repository that the agent reads at the start of every session: what the project is, how to run it, and the rules. You write it in your own words. `/init` can draft one, but yours is better because you know what is true.

This week Claude Code only explains things and, in the last lesson, finishes routes you started. Next lesson you learn to ask it well.

lessons.lesson:
### A brief for a literal colleague
A prompt to a coding agent is a brief for a very fast, very literal colleague who has never seen your project. Vague briefs produce confident guesses. Four parts turn a wish into a brief.

### The four parts
1. **Goal:** what should exist when it is done, said as an outcome, not an activity.
2. **Context:** what it needs to know about the code and the data, and no more.
3. **Constraints:** what must not change, what is off limits, which files to leave alone.
4. **How to check:** the exact thing you will run or look at to know it worked.

Written down, the check tells the agent when to stop and tells you what to look at in the diff.

### From the guide
The guide you read before this lesson adds the rest: **be clear and direct**, **give a role** when the task has a point of view, and **show one example** when the shape matters more than the words. Those are the same ideas applied to any model, and you will use them again when Triage calls Claude from code.

### Two more habits
- **One change at a time.** Small diffs are reviewable; large ones are accepted on faith.
- **Unasked changes are your prompt's fault.** Discard, add a constraint, run again.

Today you will feel the difference by giving Claude Code the vague version first.

lessons.lesson:
### A program that never finishes
A backend is a program that starts, opens a **port**, and waits. Each time a request arrives it runs the matching function, sends a response, and goes back to waiting. **Express** is the small framework that does the waiting and matching for you; you write the functions.

### Routes
A **route** is a method plus a path: `GET /api/issues`. Its function receives:
- a **request** object, with the URL, any parameters such as `:id`, and later a body;
- a **response** object you use to send JSON and a status code.

Express fills in `200` when you do not say otherwise. For a missing issue you say `404` yourself, with a small JSON body so the client knows why.

### package.json
`npm init` creates `package.json`, the file that names your project and its dependencies. `npm install express` adds Express to it and to `node_modules`, which Git must ignore. A **start script** lets anyone run the server with `npm start`, including Claude Code later.

### Why by hand
The two routes are short enough to type in ten minutes, and the point is that you can. Next lesson the data moves to a database; the lesson after, Claude Code adds the rest, and you will be able to tell whether its routes look like yours.

lessons.lesson:
### One file, no server to install
A database is a program whose only job is to keep data safe and findable. **SQLite** is the simplest kind: the whole database is one file on disk, `triage.db`, and your server opens it directly.

### Tables, rows, keys
Data lives in **tables**. A table has **columns** with names and types, and **rows** that are the records. The `issues` table has `id`, `title`, and `status`. `id` is the **primary key**: a number that identifies exactly one row, which is what `GET /api/issues/:id` needs.

### Four statements cover the week
- `CREATE TABLE` makes the table, once.
- `INSERT` adds a row.
- `SELECT` reads rows, with `WHERE` to choose which.
- `UPDATE` changes a row.

Each is a plain sentence you can read aloud, which is why SQL has lasted fifty years.

### The question mark is not decoration
From Node.js, **better-sqlite3** turns a statement into a function: `prepare` the SQL with `?` where a value goes, then `run` it with the values. If you build SQL by gluing strings together, a title containing a quote breaks the statement and a title containing SQL **runs** it. Placeholders make that impossible, and Claude Code will be told to use them next lesson.

Today's script runs on its own, not inside the server. Run it twice and watch what happens; the surprise is the lesson.

examples.caption: db-play.js: the four statements from Node.js
examples.code:
import Database from "better-sqlite3"

const db = new Database("triage.db")

db.exec(`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS issues (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open'
)`)

const insert = db.prepare("INSERT INTO issues (title) VALUES (?)")
insert.run("Login button does nothing on mobile")
insert.run("Export report as CSV")

console.log(db.prepare("SELECT * FROM issues").all())

db.prepare("UPDATE issues SET status = ? WHERE id = ?").run("done", 2)
console.log(db.prepare("SELECT * FROM issues WHERE status = ?").all("done"))

### Where the two halves meet
You know what a route looks like because you wrote two. You know what SQL looks like because you wrote four statements. Now Claude Code writes routes and SQL, and you check them against what you know.

- If the title is blank, answer `400` with `{ error }`.
- Otherwise insert with a prepared statement and answer `201` with the new row.

Test it with `curl`, because the browser cannot send a POST on its own.

2. Read the diff against it.

For each file: what changed and why, which line protects against SQL injection, and what would break if one branch were removed. Your mentor reads this at the review, and so do you. **Nothing Claude wrote stays a black box**, because you have just described it in your own words.

lessons.lesson:
### Components
React builds a screen out of **components**: functions that return what to draw. The Triage board is a tree of them: an `App` holding a `Board`, which holds an `AddIssueForm` and three `Column`s, each holding `IssueCard`s. Each lives in its own file and is imported where it is used. Small components are easy to name, test, and reuse.

### Props flow down
A parent gives a child data through **props**: `<Column title="Open" issues={open} />`. The child reads them and cannot change them. That one-way flow is the whole trick: you always know where a value came from.

### State is memory that redraws
A component remembers things with **state**, declared with `useState`. Change it through its setter and React re-renders that component and everything inside it. Change a plain variable instead and nothing happens, because React was never told. Press the buttons in the render tracer and watch which boxes light up.

### Where state lives
Put state in the **closest component above everyone who needs it**. The list of issues is needed by the columns and the form, so it lives in `Board` and flows down as props. The text being typed is needed only by the form, so it stays there. When a child must change shared state, the parent passes down a function: `onAdd`.

### Why React
Vue and Angular do the same job; React is the most used, the best documented, and one language with your server. Next lesson you type the board by hand.

options.text: So it can tell which card is which when the list changes, instead of redrawing all of them.

options.text: For styling.

options.text: It disappears, because the list is state in the browser and not yet saved through the API.

options.text: It stays, because React remembers state across refreshes.

lessons.lesson:
### The folder you are about to create
`npm create vite@latest client -- --template react` makes a React app in `triage/client`. `npm install` fetches its dependencies; `npm run dev` starts a dev server that reloads as you type. The files that matter:
- `index.html`: the one page. It loads `main.jsx`.
- `src/main.jsx`: mounts `<App />` into the page.
- `src/App.jsx`: your first component. You will replace its contents.

Everything else is configuration you will meet later.

### Four components, one file each
- `Board.jsx` owns the issues state and renders the form and three columns.
- `AddIssueForm.jsx` owns the text being typed and calls `onAdd` on submit.
- `Column.jsx` receives a title and a list and renders cards.
- `IssueCard.jsx` receives one issue and renders it, with Move and Remove buttons that call functions from props.

### Controlled inputs and keys
The form's input has `value={title}` and `onChange={(e) => setTitle(e.target.value)}`: the text lives in state, so you can refuse a blank title and clear the box after Add. Every card in a list needs a `key`, and the key is the issue `id`, never the array index.

### Local state today, API tomorrow
Today the issues array lives in `Board` with two hard-coded issues. Add, Move, and Remove change that array. Refresh and it is gone; that is expected, and next lesson fixes it by talking to your API.

lessons.summary: The board reads from your Express API with fetch in an effect. Claude Code wires the writes. You explain every change.

prepare.meaning: Send a request, check response.ok, read the JSON.
Why loading data belongs in useEffect and what the dependency array means.
GET to read, POST to create, PATCH to change, DELETE to remove. You built all four.

keyReading.why: Fetching inside render is the classic beginner bug. This page explains the effect, the dependency array, and cleanup, which you need before the board can load from the API.

And when they press Add, which request should go, and should the card appear before or after the server answers?

checks.question: Where does the initial GET /api/issues belong?

options.text: In the Add button's handler.
options.feedback: That fetches only when someone adds. The page needs its data on open.

options.text: In a useEffect with an empty dependency array, so it runs once after the first render.
options.feedback: Yes. Render draws; the effect fetches after; the setter updates state; React redraws with the data.

options.text: Directly in the component body, so it runs on every render.
options.feedback: Every render would fetch again, and setting state re-renders, so it loops forever.

checks.question: The dev server runs on 5173 and the API on 3000. The fetch to /api/issues fails. Why?

options.text: The API is broken.
options.feedback: curl still works. The browser is asking the wrong server.

options.text: React cannot call APIs.
options.feedback: It can. fetch is a browser function; React just decides when to call it.

options.text: Different ports are different origins; a Vite proxy forwards /api to 3000 during development.
options.feedback: Right. In production one server serves both; in development the proxy stands in for that.

checks.question: After POST succeeds the server returns the new issue with its id. What should the board do?

options.text: Add the returned issue to state, so the card has the real id.
options.feedback: Yes. The server owns ids. Using its reply keeps the board and the database in agreement.

options.text: Refresh the page.
options.feedback: Refreshing works but throws away everything else on screen. Update state instead.

options.text: Add the typed title to state before sending, and ignore the reply.
options.feedback: Then the card has no id and Move and Remove cannot address it. Use the reply.

lessons.lesson:
### Fetch after render
A component draws first, then loads. `useEffect(() => { ... }, [])` runs once after the first render: inside it, `fetch("/api/issues")`, check `response.ok`, read the JSON, and put it in state with the setter. React redraws with the real issues. Fetching in the component body instead would re-fetch on every render and loop forever.

### Two servers in development
Vite serves the React app on port 5173; your API listens on 3000. The browser treats different ports as different places, so `/api/issues` would go to Vite and 404. A **proxy** in `vite.config.js` forwards `/api` to 3000 during development. In production one server serves both.

### Writes use the reply
When someone presses Add, send `POST /api/issues` with the title as JSON. The server validates, inserts, and replies with the new row **including its id**. Put that reply into state; the card now has the real id, so Move (`PATCH`) and Remove (`DELETE`) can address it.

### By hand, then with the agent
You write the GET yourself: the effect, the proxy, the loading state. Then Claude Code wires POST, PATCH, and DELETE in plan mode, one at a time, and you read each diff against what you would have written. Then you explain it back.

lessons.title: Tests, fail first
lessons.summary: A test is a written expectation. Write one for the API and one for a component, see them fail, and make them pass with the smallest change.

prepare.meaning: node --test, describe, it, assert. No install needed for the API side.
The test runner for the React side. Same shape, different import.
Find elements the way a user would: by visible text and labels.

keyReading.why: Its guiding principle, test what the user sees, decides how you write the component test today and every one after.

lessons.predictPrompt: Triage has a rule nobody wrote down: once an issue is Done, it must not be moved back to Open. Right now the API would happily allow it. You are going to write a test for that rule before the rule exists. What do you think the test will do when you run it: pass, fail, or error? What should you see change after you add the rule, without touching the test? And what would it mean if the test passed on the very first run?

checks.question: You write a test for the done-to-open rule and it passes on the first run, before the rule exists. What does that tell you?

options.text: The test is not testing what you think. A test must fail first to prove it can.
options.feedback: Yes. Red first is the proof. A test that cannot fail guards nothing.

options.text: The rule was already there.
options.feedback: Check the code: nothing rejects the move. The test is wrong, not the code.

options.text: Node is caching the result.
options.feedback: Tests do not cache. Read the assertion again.

checks.question: What does a green test prove?

options.text: That the code is well written.
options.feedback: A test checks behaviour, not style. Ugly code passes tests too.

options.text: That this one expectation holds for this one case. Nothing about cases you did not write.
options.feedback: Right. Tests are specific. Name what each does not cover and you know where the next one goes.

options.text: That the feature has no bugs.
options.feedback: It proves one case. A second case can still be broken.

checks.question: In a component test, which query is best?

options.text: document.querySelector(".btn-primary").
options.feedback: A class name is an implementation detail. Rename the class and the test breaks for no reason.

options.text: The second button in the DOM.
options.feedback: Position changes constantly. Query by meaning.

options.text: getByRole("button", { name: "Add" }), because that is what a user sees and a screen reader announces.
options.feedback: Yes. Query by role and visible text, so the test survives a CSS or structure change.

lessons.lesson:
### A test is a written expectation
A test calls your code and asserts what should happen. `node --test` runs the API tests with no install. **Vitest** and **Testing Library** run the React tests. Both have the same shape: arrange, act, assert.

### Fail first
Write the test for a rule **before** the rule exists and run it. It must go **red**. That red run proves the test can fail, which is the only reason to trust it when it is green. Then make the smallest change that turns it green. Then ask what the test does **not** prove, and write the next one.

### What to test on each side
- **API:** rules. A done issue cannot move back to open; a blank title is refused with 400; a new issue starts open.
- **Component:** what the user sees. Typing a title and pressing Add shows a new card; a blank title shows the message.

Query elements the way a user finds them: by role and visible text, never by class name or position.

### By hand, then with the agent
You write both tests by hand and watch them fail. Claude Code makes the API test pass with the smallest change, and you check that it did not touch the test. Then you explain the change back.

  render(<AddIssueForm onAdd={() => {}} />)
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Add" }))
  expect(screen.getByRole("alert")).toHaveTextContent("A title is required.")
})

lessons.title: States and usability
lessons.summary: Empty, loading, error, success. Make the board honest about what is happening and usable without a mouse.

prepare.meaning: Keyboard users, screen reader users, and everyone on a slow connection.
Real buttons, labels on inputs, headings in order.
List the visual states first, then let state drive them.

keyReading.why: Before you write the eight states, understand who the board shuts out when it needs a mouse or hides an error. This page names them.

lessons.predictPrompt: Imagine opening Triage on a slow train connection. The page appears but the columns are empty for five seconds, then the issues arrive. Now imagine the server is down: the columns stay empty forever. In both cases the screen looked the same. What do you think the person concluded each time, and what should the board have said instead? Then try your own board with the mouse unplugged: can you add an issue using only the keyboard?

checks.question: The columns are empty. What are the two different things that could mean?

options.text: The server is down.
options.feedback: That is a third state, error, and it needs its own words too.

options.text: The CSS is broken.
options.feedback: Possibly, but the board's own states come first: empty, loading, error, success.

options.text: There are no issues, or the issues have not loaded. The board must show which.
options.feedback: Yes. 'No issues yet' and 'Loading…' are different states with different words.

checks.question: Add fails because the server refused. What should happen to the title the person typed?

options.text: It stays in the box, with the message next to it, so they can fix and retry.
options.feedback: Right. Clearing the input on failure punishes the person for the server's problem.

options.text: The box is cleared so they can start again.
options.feedback: They lose their work. Keep the input on failure, clear it on success.

options.text: The page reloads.
options.feedback: A reload hides what went wrong and loses the text.

checks.question: Why use a real button element instead of a styled div with onClick?

options.text: Buttons are faster.
options.feedback: Speed is not the point. Keyboard and screen reader support is.

options.text: A button is focusable, works with Enter and Space, and is announced as a button. A div is none of those.
options.feedback: Yes. Semantics are free accessibility. Use the element that means what you mean.

options.text: Divs cannot have click handlers.
options.feedback: They can, which is the trap: it works with a mouse and nothing else.

lessons.lesson:
### Four states every screen has
- **Loading:** the request is out. Say so: 'Loading issues…'.
- **Empty:** it worked and there is nothing. Say so: 'No issues yet. Add the first one.'
- **Error:** it failed. Say what and offer a retry: 'Could not load issues. Try again.'
- **Success:** the data, plus any pending state while a write is in flight.

A board that shows blank columns for all four is lying by omission. Write the exact words for each state **before** you touch code; the words are the specification.

### Writes have states too
Pressing Add starts a request. While it is pending, disable the button so it cannot be pressed twice. On success, clear the input. On failure, **keep the input** and show the message next to it. The same for Move and Remove.

### Usable without a mouse
Use a real `<button>`, a real `<form>`, and a `<label>` or `aria-label` on every input. Then unplug the mouse: Tab should reach everything in a sensible order, Enter should submit, and the message for an error should be announced, which `role="alert"` does.

### By hand, then with the agent
You list the eight states and their words, and you find out by hand what the board does today with the server stopped. Claude Code implements the states one flow at a time from your list; you verify each with the server stopped, with an empty database, and with the keyboard only.

Could not load issues.

No issues yet. Add the first one.

To test the error state, stop the server, not the whole machine. To test empty, delete the rows, not the table.
Tab order follows the order in the HTML. If Add comes before the input in the markup, the keyboard path is backwards.

prepare.meaning: What a pull request is and what a reviewer sees.
The clicks from a pushed branch to an open request.
Added, removed, and context lines. You will read your own week this way.

checks.question: What does a pull request description need?

options.feedback: Code says what; only you can say why and how you checked.

options.text: What changed, why, how you checked it, and what you want the reviewer to look at.

checks.question: Claude Code reviews your branch and lists six risks. What do you do?

options.text: Decide on each one: fix now, write down for later, or disagree with a reason. Add at most one fix in a new commit.
options.feedback: Right. A review is input, not instructions. You judge; you stay the author.

checks.question: Why never commit directly to main?

options.text: So every change is reviewed before it reaches the version that works.
options.feedback: Yes. A branch is a safe place to be wrong. main is the place that must not be.

options.text: Because GitHub forbids it.
options.feedback: It allows it unless protected. The rule is yours and your team's.

options.text: Branches are faster to push.

lessons.lesson:
### The week on a branch
Everything you did this week is on `board`, in small commits whose messages say the outcome. `main` has not changed. A **pull request** asks for `board` to be reviewed and merged into `main`. Run the playground to see the steps.

### The description is the review's map
Write it in your own words under four headings:
- **What changed:** the board, the API wiring, the tests, the states.
- **Why:** the week's brief, in one sentence.
- **How I checked it:** what you ran and what you saw, including the server-stopped and keyboard-only checks.
- **Look at:** the two places you are least sure of.

Your mentor has thirty minutes. The description decides where they go.

### Two reviews, one author
Ask Claude Code to review the diff of `board` against `main`: risks, missing tests, unclear names. Then **judge** each item: fix now, note for later, or disagree with a reason. Add at most one fix, in a new commit, and do not let it rewrite your description. Your mentor's review comes next; Week 4 opens by responding to it.

### What merges
Nothing yet. The request stays open until your mentor's review is answered.

lessons.title: SOLID, in plain words
lessons.summary: Five principles, one Triage-sized example each. Learn to name what is wrong with a piece of code before you fix it.

prepare.meaning: Single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion. Read it once; the lesson translates.
The catalogue of changes that keep behaviour and improve shape. Skim the first page.

keyReading.why: The standard explanation of all five principles with short examples. Read it before the sorter; the lesson only translates each one into Triage.

widgets.title: Which principle is being broken?
widgets.instruction: Each card describes a piece of Triage code. Decide which SOLID principle it breaks. Read the five first.

buckets.name: Single responsibility
buckets.meaning: A module has one reason to change.

buckets.name: Open/closed
buckets.meaning: Add behaviour by adding code, not by editing what works.

buckets.name: Liskov substitution
buckets.meaning: Anything that stands in for something else must honour its promises.

buckets.name: Interface segregation
buckets.meaning: Do not force a caller to depend on things it does not use.

buckets.name: Dependency inversion
buckets.meaning: High-level rules should not depend on low-level details; both depend on an agreement.

cards.text: The POST route validates the title, writes SQL, and formats the JSON reply, all in one function.
cards.why: Three reasons to change in one place: validation rules, storage, and response shape. Split them.

cards.text: Adding a Blocked status means editing a long if/else chain in three files.
cards.why: A table of allowed moves lets you add a row instead of editing branches. Add, do not edit.

cards.text: A test double for the database returns undefined where the real one throws on a missing id.
cards.why: The stand-in breaks the promise of the thing it replaces, so tests pass and production fails.

cards.text: Every route receives the whole db object even though each uses one function.

lessons.lesson:
### Five principles, one sentence each
- **S, single responsibility:** a module has one reason to change.
- **O, open/closed:** add behaviour by adding code, not by editing code that works.
- **L, Liskov substitution:** anything that stands in for something else must keep its promises.
- **I, interface segregation:** do not make a caller depend on things it does not use.
- **D, dependency inversion:** high-level rules should not depend on low-level details; both depend on an agreement.

### The same five, in Triage
- **S:** your POST route validates, writes SQL, and shapes the reply. Three reasons to change. Next lesson they become three layers.
- **O:** the status rule as a chain of ifs must be edited for every new status. As a table of allowed moves, a new status is a new row.
- **L:** a fake database used in tests must behave like the real one: throw where it throws, return what it returns.
- **I:** a route that needs `listIssues` should receive `listIssues`, not the whole database object.
- **D:** the status rule should not import `better-sqlite3`. It should be given the current status and decide. The driver is a detail.

### Why name them
Naming a problem is most of fixing it. 'This function has three reasons to change' tells a reviewer, and Claude Code, exactly what to do. Vague discomfort does not.

### Two more words you will hear
**DRY**, don't repeat yourself: a rule lives in one place. **Name for intent:** a reader should know what a function does without opening it. They are not in SOLID, and they matter just as much.

lessons.lesson:
### Three layers
- `routes/` speaks **HTTP**: reads the request, calls the service, writes the status and body. No rules, no SQL.
- `service/` holds the **rules**: validation, the status table, what a new issue starts as. No Express, no SQL.
- `db/` speaks **SQL**: prepared statements, one function per statement. No rules.

### The dependency rule
Dependencies point **inwards**, towards the rules. Routes import the service. The service calls data functions it is given, or imports a small data module that knows nothing about rules. Nothing in `service/` mentions `req`, `res`, or `better-sqlite3`. That is what lets you test a rule in a millisecond with no database file.

### The status rule, once
`service/status.js` owns the table of allowed moves and one function, `canMove(from, to)`. Every route that changes status asks it. Adding Blocked next month is a new row and a new test, nowhere else.

### How to move code without breaking it
Tests green. Extract one function. Tests green. Move it to its layer. Tests green. If a step goes red, that step changed behaviour: undo and take a smaller one. You extract the first function by hand; Claude Code does the rest in plan mode, running the tests after every step; you explain it back.

lessons.lesson:
### Four kinds of comment
Sort every comment before you act:
- **Bug:** something is wrong. Fix first, with a test.
- **Clarity:** a name or shape is confusing. Usually worth doing; it is cheap now and expensive later.
- **Question:** the reviewer wants to understand. Answer in writing; sometimes the answer is a comment in the code.
- **Preference:** a matter of taste. Do it if it is free, decline with a reason if not.

### Reply to every one
A review is a conversation. Each comment gets a written reply: what you did, or why you did not. Then an action list of the agreed changes, **one commit per comment**, each message naming what it answers. The reviewer re-reads the thread, not the whole diff.

### Giving comments
When it is your turn, write comments someone can act on: a location, a consequence, a suggestion. 'Line 42: untrimmed title lets whitespace through; a test for it would catch this.' Not 'messy'. Say which kind each comment is, so the author knows what to prioritise.

### With the agent
Work through the action list with Claude Code, one item per commit, then ask it to check your new commits against the original comments and say whether each is addressed. Where it disagrees with you, decide, and say why in the thread.

options.feedback: Yes. package.json says 'about this version'; the lockfile says 'exactly this one'. CI relies on it.

options.text: You should not; it is generated.
options.feedback: Generated, and still committed. It is the record of what actually ran.

options.text: It makes installs faster.
options.feedback: Sometimes, but the point is sameness, not speed.

checks.question: Where does the database path belong?

options.text: In .env, committed to the repository.

options.text: In the environment (DB_PATH), with a sensible default and .env.example listing the name without a value.
options.feedback: Right. The code stays the same on every machine; the environment changes.

options.text: Hard-coded, so nobody can misconfigure it.
options.feedback: Then the team server needs a code change to use a different path. Configuration is not code.

lessons.lesson:
### Same code, different machine
Three things differ between two machines running the same repository:
- **Dependency versions.** `package.json` says roughly which; `package-lock.json` says exactly which. Commit the lockfile and `npm ci` installs exactly that.
- **Environment:** the port, the database path, keys. These must not be in code.
- **The Node.js version** itself. `.nvmrc` records it.

### Configuration lives in the environment
`PORT` and `DB_PATH` come from `process.env`, with sensible defaults for development. `.env` holds your machine's values and is in `.gitignore`. `.env.example` holds the **names only** and is committed, so a new teammate knows what to set. If a required value is missing or points somewhere impossible, the server should **fail fast at startup** with a clear message, not crash later with a confusing one.

### Secrets
A key in a commit is a leaked key, even if the file was deleted in the next commit: **history is forever**. The response is always: rotate the key, then clean up. GitHub's secret scanning will often tell you first; do not wait for it.

### By hand, then with the agent
You find the exact Express version in the lockfile, write `.env.example`, and hunt a planted secret in a sample repository your mentor provides. Claude Code moves the configuration into the environment with fail-fast checks, and you explain it back.

lessons.lesson:
### Four words
A **workflow** is a file in `.github/workflows/`. It runs **jobs** on a **runner**, a fresh machine GitHub starts for you. Each job is a list of **steps**: check out the code, install Node, install dependencies, run the tests. Press the pipeline tracer to watch one push go through.

### Why the lockfile and .nvmrc matter now
The runner has nothing of yours. `actions/setup-node` with `node-version-file: .nvmrc` gives it your Node. `npm ci` installs exactly the lockfile's versions. Without those two, CI tests a different machine from the one you develop on, and the first run teaches you that the hard way.

### What green proves
Green means **the tests you wrote pass on a clean machine**. It does not prove the feature works, that the code is reviewed, that the board is usable with a keyboard, or anything you did not write a test for. Say out loud what your workflow does not check; that is next week's test list.

### Red is information
A red run names the step and prints the error. Read the first real error line. Environment problems (Node version, missing lockfile) look like code problems until you read them.

### By hand, then with the agent
You write the workflow file from the quickstart, predict what the first run shows, and push. If it is red, Claude Code helps you read the error and fix the environment difference. Then it adds a second check, such as the client tests or a lint step, and you explain it back.

examples.caption: .github/workflows/test.yml
examples.code:
name: tests
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
      - run: npm ci
      - run: node --test
      - run: npm --prefix client ci && npm --prefix client test

Then ask it to add one more check to the workflow, such as a lint step, and to say what the workflow still does not check. Add at least two of those gaps to `notes.txt`. Explain it back.

lessons.lesson:
### Image, container, volume
A **Dockerfile** is a recipe: start from a Node image, copy `package*.json`, `npm ci`, copy the code, build the client, declare the command. `docker build` turns it into an **image**: everything frozen. `docker run` starts a **container** from it. Containers are disposable; the database is not, so `triage.db` lives in a **volume** mounted into the container, and `DB_PATH` points there. `.dockerignore` keeps `node_modules`, `.env`, and `*.db` out of the image.

### Compose and the environment
`docker-compose.yml` says in one file what `docker run` needs: the image, the port, the volume, and the environment. Secrets and paths come from an env file on the server, never from the image. Last lesson's fail-fast check is what tells you when the server's environment is wrong.

### A server and a proxy
On the team server: pull the repository, build the image, `docker compose up -d`. A **reverse proxy** such as Caddy answers on 443 with HTTPS and forwards to your container on 3000. Your app never sees a certificate. This is **CD**, continuous delivery, in its simplest form: a repeatable script that puts a tested image where people can use it.

### By hand, then with the agent, then with your mentor
You write the Dockerfile and `.dockerignore` by hand and run the image locally with a volume. Claude Code writes the deploy script and explains every command you do not recognise. Your mentor is at the keyboard for the server itself; you say what each command does before it runs.

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
COPY client/package*.json ./client/
RUN npm ci && npm --prefix client ci
COPY . .
RUN npm --prefix client run build
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

services:
  triage:
    build: .
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      DB_PATH: /data/triage.db
    volumes: ["triage-data:/data"]
    restart: unless-stopped

  triage-data:

lessons.lesson:
### Three ways to label
- **Rules:** a developer writes `if title includes "crash" then bug`. Cheap, predictable, limited.
- **Machine learning:** a model learns from thousands of labelled issues and outputs a label. Needs data you do not have.
- **Generative AI:** a language model reads the title and writes a label and a reason. Flexible, costs money per call, can be wrong with confidence.

Triage will use rules first, then the model, with rules as the fallback.

### The rules version
`service/labeler.js` takes a title and returns `{ label, priority, source: "rules" }`. Keyword lists: crash, error, broken, 'does nothing' lean bug; add, export, support, 'would be nice' lean feature. Priority from words like urgent, blocked, production. Write it by hand; it is the baseline.

### The test set
Fifteen realistic titles with the label and priority **you** expect, in `test/issues.json`. Include two that are deliberately vague. Keep five of them back from tuning so you still have something to measure with. A score is only a measurement if the examples were not used to build the thing being scored.

### Scoring
A small script runs the labeler over the set and prints expected versus actual with a count of misses. The same script scores the model in two lessons, and the comparison goes into your pull request description.

lessons.lesson:
### Four surfaces
- **Claude Code:** the agent on your machine, driven by you. For building software.
- **Direct API:** your code sends one request, with a key, a model name, and messages, and gets one reply. The **Claude API** and the **OpenAI API** both work this way; the field names differ, the idea does not. This is what Triage uses.
- **Cloud platform:** the same API reached through **Microsoft Foundry**, **Amazon Bedrock**, or **Google Vertex AI**, because the company wants billing, keys, data location, and audit in one place. The prompt and the reply are the same; the client and the authentication change.
- **Agent SDK:** the loop from Week 2, read, decide, act, observe, with tools, running as part of your product without you. Claude Code's engine, available to your own code.

### How to choose
Ask three questions. **Does it need to act**, or just answer? Answer: direct API. Act with tools over many steps: Agent SDK. **Who is at the keyboard?** You: Claude Code. Nobody: API or SDK. **Where may the data go?** Anywhere the provider allows: direct. Only inside the company's cloud: the platform.

### What this means for Triage
The suggest endpoint is one request, one structured reply: the direct Claude API, next lesson. If your company required Foundry, `service/assistant.js` would swap the client and keep the prompt. If one day Triage files issues on its own from test failures, that is an Agent SDK job.

lessons.lesson:
### One request
`service/assistant.js` makes a single call to the Messages API with four things: the **model**, **max_tokens**, a **system prompt** that says what the model is and what to return, and a **user message** with the issue title. The reply is text; next lesson you make it a fixed shape. The function returns `{ label, priority, source: "model" }` so the rest of Triage cannot tell rules from model except by that field.

### The key
The SDK reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment. It goes in `.env` on your machine, in the server's env file in production, and in `.env.example` as a name with no value. It never appears in code, in a prompt, in a log line, in a commit, or in the question log. Your mentor gives you the key through the approved channel.

### Cost and limits
Each request costs by tokens in and out. A label needs a short system prompt and `max_tokens` around 100. Fifty issues a day at that size is pennies; a loop that retries forever is not. Count requests in a log line that contains no key and no title.

### The endpoint
`POST /api/issues/:id/suggest` loads the issue, calls the assistant, and returns the suggestion. It does not store anything yet; the decision comes in the last lesson. By hand you write the request on paper and the `.env.example` line; Claude Code adds the SDK with a reason in the commit message, the service, and the route; you explain it back.

checks.question: The API returns a rate-limit error. What should the person see?

options.feedback: Could be minutes. Fall back now, retry later if at all.

options.feedback: Length costs tokens. The example earns its place by making the output predictable.

options.text: The model cannot work without one.

options.feedback: Yes. One example of the output is worth a paragraph of instructions.

lessons.lesson:
### A prompt is part of the product
The system prompt has five parts: the **role**, the **task**, the **allowed values**, what to do **when unsure**, and the exact **output shape**. Build it in the widget. One worked example in the prompt does more than a paragraph of rules.

### Structured output
Ask for JSON that matches a schema, and the reply arrives as a fixed shape your code can read without guessing. That handles **shape**. It does not handle **meaning**: the schema cannot know that 'enhancement' is not one of your labels. Your code validates every value against the allowed set, and anything outside it is treated as no suggestion.

### Errors are different from each other
- **Rate limit or overload:** try once more after a short wait, then fall back to rules.
- **Bad request:** your code is wrong; log it without the title, fall back, and fix it.
- **Refusal or empty reply:** no suggestion; fall back.

In every case the person can still file the issue. The suggestion is extra; the board is the job.

### Cost
Count requests. Set `max_tokens` to what a label needs. Never call the model on every keystroke; call it once when the issue is created. A log line per call, with no key and no title, tells you what a month costs.

### Measure
Run the score script from L25 over all fifteen issues with the model and record the numbers next to the rules. The comparison goes in your pull request description, with the two titles where you disagreed with the model.

lessons.summary: CLAUDE.md holds standing rules. A skill holds a reusable procedure. Write one of each for Triage, from real experience.

prepare.meaning: How standing instructions are found and what belongs in them.
A folder with a SKILL.md: a procedure the agent can pick up when it fits.

keyReading.why: Read what a skill is and how it is discovered before you write one. The structure is small; the discipline is in the steps.

lessons.predictPrompt: Over four weeks you have corrected Claude Code about the same things more than once: use placeholders in SQL, one route per plan, do not touch the tests. And you have done one procedure by hand several times: turn a failing test into a clearly written issue. checks.question: What belongs in CLAUDE.md?

options.text: A diary of what Claude Code did each day.
options.feedback: History lives in git. CLAUDE.md is instructions.

options.text: Every rule you can think of.
options.feedback: Long files get skimmed, by people and by models. Keep the rules you actually needed.

options.text: Standing rules and facts about the project that are true every session: how to run it, what never to do, conventions.
options.feedback: Yes. Short, true, and maintained. A rule you no longer follow is worse than no rule.

checks.question: What is a skill?

options.text: A written procedure with steps, in a SKILL.md, that the agent picks up when a task matches its description.
options.feedback: Right. Rules say what is always true; a skill says how to do one kind of job well.

options.text: A plugin you install from a store.
options.feedback: A skill is a folder in your repository. You write it.

options.text: A model fine-tuned on your code.
options.feedback: No training. It is text the agent reads.

checks.question: The skill produced an issue that skipped your 'steps to reproduce' section. What do you fix?

options.text: Nothing; the model is unreliable.
options.feedback: Ambiguous steps get varied results. Precise steps get consistent ones.

options.text: The skill's step that was ambiguous. Then run it again on the same failure.
options.feedback: Yes. Treat a skill like code: when the output is wrong, the instruction was unclear. Fix the instruction.

options.text: The output, by hand, every time.
options.feedback: Then the skill saves nothing. Fix it once.

lessons.lesson:
### Rules versus procedures
**CLAUDE.md** holds what is always true: how to run Triage, that SQL uses placeholders, that tests are never edited to pass, that one plan touches one route. The agent reads it at the start of every session. Keep it short and keep it true; remove a rule the moment it stops being true.

A **skill** is a procedure: a folder under `.claude/skills/` with a `SKILL.md` that says when it applies and the exact steps. The agent picks it up when a task matches. Rules are read every time; skills are used when they fit.

### Rules learned
Add a 'Rules learned' section to CLAUDE.md with three rules you actually needed this month, each from a real correction you made. Delete anything stale. A CLAUDE.md that says the project is `hello.js` is a lie the agent will believe.

### A skill for Triage
`.claude/skills/issue-from-test/SKILL.md`: given a failing test's output, write a Triage issue with a title under ten words, the exact failing assertion, steps to reproduce, and a suggested label. Write the steps by hand, as you would do them. Then break a test on purpose, paste the failure, and watch the skill produce an issue. Where the output drifts from your steps, the step was ambiguous: fix it and run again.

examples.caption: .claude/skills/issue-from-test/SKILL.md
examples.code:
---
name: issue-from-test
description: Turn a failing test's output into a Triage issue with a reproducible report.
---

When given failing test output:
1. Title: under ten words, naming the behaviour, not the test. Example: "Done issue can be reopened".
2. Quote the exact failing assertion line.
3. Steps to reproduce: the command and the inputs, numbered.
4. Suggested label (bug) and priority (high if production, otherwise normal) with one-line reasoning.
5. Output as JSON matching POST /api/issues, nothing else.

lessons.title: The triage assistant
lessons.summary: Ship the suggestion with a human decision in front of it. The model drafts; the person decides.

prepare.meaning: The board must work with the model switched off. Reread what each error means.

lessons.predictPrompt: Someone files 'Checkout page freezes on Safari'. A second later a suggestion appears: bug, high, with a reason. They can accept it, change it, or dismiss it. checks.question: Why store the decision with its source?

options.text: You should not store suggestions.
options.feedback: Store the decision and where it came from. That is the whole value of a human in front of the model.

options.text: So you can measure later: how often the model's suggestion was accepted, changed, or dismissed, versus rules.
options.feedback: Yes. 'Decided by person, suggested by model, accepted' is a row you can count. Without it, the feature is unmeasurable.

options.text: For legal reasons.
options.feedback: Maybe one day. Today it is so you can learn whether the model earns its cost.

checks.question: The model is down. What does filing an issue look like?

options.text: A banner saying the AI is unavailable.
options.feedback: They did not come for the AI. A small 'no suggestion' is enough.

options.text: Filing is blocked until the model returns.
options.feedback: Never. The board must not depend on the model.

options.text: Exactly like a normal day, with the rules suggestion or none, and nothing red on screen.
options.feedback: Right. The person's job is filing. The assistant is optional, and its absence is quiet.

checks.question: Why is 'change' a separate decision from 'accept' and 'dismiss'?

options.text: Because a changed suggestion was useful but wrong, which is different from useless, and you want to count both.
options.feedback: Yes. Three outcomes tell you three different things about the prompt.

options.text: It is not; change is just dismiss plus a new label.
options.feedback: Functionally close, but the record is different, and the record is the point.

options.text: To make the interface bigger.
options.feedback: Three small buttons. The reason is the data, not the screen.

lessons.lesson:
### The flow
When an issue is created, Triage asks the assistant: model first, rules as fallback. The card shows the suggestion with three buttons: **Accept**, **Change**, **Dismiss**. Until the person decides, the issue has no label. When they decide, Triage stores the label, the priority, and the **source and outcome**: suggested by model or rules, accepted, changed, or dismissed.

### Four states
- **Suggesting:** the request is out; the card shows 'Suggesting…' and the buttons are hidden.
- **Suggested:** label, priority, reason, three buttons.
- **Unavailable:** no suggestion arrived; the card offers a plain label picker.
- **Decided:** the label, with a small note of where it came from.

Draw them before you write them; the words come from your L17 habit.

### The model is down
This is the test your mentor will run: stop the model (a wrong key is enough) and file an issue. Filing works, the rules suggestion or none appears, nothing is red. If that fails, the feature is not done.

### The record
A `suggestions` table: issue id, suggested label and priority, source, outcome, decided at. Next month, one query says how often the model was accepted, changed, or dismissed. That number decides whether the model keeps its place.

examples.caption: The suggestions table
examples.code:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS suggestions (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  issue_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  label TEXT NOT NULL,
  priority TEXT NOT NULL,
  source TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (source IN ('model', 'rules')),
  outcome TEXT CHECK (outcome IN ('accepted', 'changed', 'dismissed')),
  decided_at TEXT
);

Add tests for the fallback and for each decision. Run your test plan, including with a wrong key. Open the week's pull request with the measured scores in the description. Explain it back.

Add PATCH /api/suggestions/:id with { outcome, label?, priority? } for accepted, changed, dismissed, which sets the issue's label and priority and records decided_at. The board shows the four states with these words: [paste]. The board must work unchanged when the model fails. Tell me the files before editing.

With a wrong key, filing an issue works and shows the rules suggestion or none, with nothing red.
Tests cover the fallback and each decision; CI is green on the pull request; the scores are in the description.

hints: Ask for the model call to be awaited without blocking the response if it is slow; the issue should exist before the suggestion does.
Test the unavailable state first. It is the one that embarrasses you in a demo.
If the card shows a suggestion but no buttons, the state is 'suggested' without its decision handlers. Check what the card received as props.

lessons.lesson:
### What you are doing this week
You are adding **one more feature to your own Triage app**, the one you have built since Week 2. There are no step-by-step instructions this time: you get the requirements, and you plan and build it the way you learned in Weeks 2 to 5. Your mentor reviews the result.

### Today: choose and describe
1. Read the three features in the widget below and **pick one**. Each has a numbered list of requirements. Those requirements are what "done" means.
2. Write a short file, `docs/feature.md` (what goes in it is listed below).
3. Post it in the question log and ask your mentor to agree it.

### What docs/feature.md contains
- **The feature name** and its numbered requirements, copied from the widget.
- **One sentence on who it helps**: for example, "a teammate can see which issues are waiting on someone else".
- **One thing you will not build**: for per-user boards, "no login".
- **The files you expect to change**, and the one you are least sure about.

### Then: look, but do not touch
Open Claude Code in **plan mode** and ask it to list the files it would change for your feature. Compare with your list. Where the lists differ, open the file and decide who is right. **Nothing is edited today.** Building starts next lesson.

### How to build it
Work through your numbered requirements **one at a time**, each one all the way through: the rule, the API, the database if needed, the board, and a test.

1. **Requirement 1 by hand.** Create a branch named after the feature. Build the first requirement yourself, with its test, and commit. For the Blocked column that is: add the row to the status table, write the test, make the API accept the move.
2. **The rest with Claude Code, one plan per requirement.** For each remaining requirement: plan mode, read the plan against your file list, approve, read the diff, run the tests, try it in the browser, commit. If a plan touches a file not on your list, ask why first.
3. **Open the pull request.** Description under the four headings from Week 3, plus your numbered requirements with how you checked each one. Get CI green.
4. **Explain it back** below: every file Claude Code changed, what and why.

### Keep steps small
If one requirement takes more than an hour, split it. Commit what works. A small bad step is cheap to throw away.

All requirements working, tests for the rules, CI green, and your Explain it back. Not polish.

lessons.lesson:
### What to write
Create `docs/HANDOVER.md` with four sections, in this order:

1. **Run it.** Every command from a fresh clone to a working board, in order, and what you should see after each one. Type each command in a fresh terminal while you write, and paste it from there.
2. **Check it.** How to run both test suites, what green looks like, and what CI checks and does not check.
3. **How it is built.** One short paragraph each: the three layers of the server, the status table, the assistant and its fallback, where the database file lives in production.
4. **Continue it.** How to add a new status, how to change the assistant's prompt, where your last feature stopped, and the three things you would do next.

### Names, never values
List every environment variable by name and say who provides the value. No keys, passwords, or tokens anywhere, not even old ones.

### Test it on a person
Give the document to one person (not your mentor) and ask them to follow only **Run it**. Watch where they stop. Fix that line. That is the whole review.

### With Claude Code
Ask it to read the document as a new teammate and list the questions they would still have. Decide which are real. Answer those in your own words. Do not let it rewrite the document.

examples.caption: Run it, as it should read
examples.code:
## Run it
1. `git clone git@github.com:you/triage.git && cd triage`
2. `nvm use` (Node version is in .nvmrc)
3. `cp .env.example .env` and set DB_PATH=./triage.db. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ask the mentor. The board works without it.
4. `npm ci && npm --prefix client ci`
5. `npm start` in one terminal, `npm --prefix client run dev` in another
6. Open http://localhost:5173. You should see three columns and two seeded issues.

### Start with a person
The first thirty seconds are about a teammate with a problem: issues lost in chat, nobody sure what is blocked. Then show the board. Then, briefly, what it took to build. The code comes last, and only one piece of it.

### Write an outline with minute marks
- **0:00** the person and the problem
- **1:00** the board: file an issue, move it, see the suggestion, decide
- **3:00** your last feature, and one thing that was hard
- **5:00** one piece of code that shows a decision you made, on screen for under a minute
- **6:00** what you would do next
- **7:00** questions

Rehearse once with a timer and write down the real time. Cut until it fits.

### Make a fallback
Record the two-minute flow, or take four screenshots. If the live demo fails, switch to it without comment.

### Prepare for questions
Ask Claude Code, as the audience, for the three questions an engineer would ask afterwards. Prepare honest answers. 'I do not know yet; here is how I would find out' is a complete answer.

examples.caption: The one piece of code, with its one sentence

### Part 1: the demo (five to ten minutes)
Give the demo from your outline. Fallback ready. Answer questions honestly, including 'I do not know yet; here is how I would find out'.

### Part 2: explain one part of your code (about fifteen minutes)
Every AI tool closed. No notes. Your mentor picks one thing a person does on the board, for example **add an issue**, and you explain out loud everything that happens, in order:
- the form's submit handler in `AddIssueForm.jsx`
- the request it sends (method, path, body)
- the route in `routes/issues.js`
- the rule in `service/issues.js`
- the prepared statement in `db/issues.js`
- the reply, the state update in `Board.jsx`, and the new card on screen

For each step: the file, and roughly where in it. Where you are not sure, say so, and say where you would look.

### What is being judged
Three things, the same as in Week 1: can you **explain** it, could you **change** it, and can you **predict** what a change would do. Not polish.

### Afterwards
Write down the two questions you handled worst. They start next lesson's reflection.

examples.caption: An explanation, as it should sound
examples.code:
"Add is a form submit in AddIssueForm.jsx. It calls onAdd from Board.jsx, which sends POST /api/issues with { title }.
routes/issues.js reads the body and calls createIssue in service/issues.js, which checks the title is not blank and asks the assistant for a suggestion.
db/issues.js runs the INSERT with a ? placeholder and returns the row.
The route answers 201 with the row; Board puts it in state; the Open column re-renders with the new card.
Where I'm least sure: whether the suggestion is awaited before or after the 201. I'd read createIssue in service/issues.js."

byHand.task: Give your demo to the team. Then, with every AI tool closed and no notes, explain one click on the board to your mentor, step by step through the code, and answer their questions. Where you do not know, say so and say where you would look. Afterwards, write down the two questions you handled worst.
checklist: I gave the demo within the time, with the fallback ready.
I explained one click end to end with every AI tool closed.
Where I did not know, I said so and said where I would look.
I wrote down the two questions I handled worst.

hints: Say the file name before the function name. It anchors both of you.
If you lose the thread, go back to the request: method, path, body. The server side starts there.
This is not a memory test. It is a test of whether you know where to look.
lessons.reflection: Which step did you know best, and in which week did you learn it?

lessons.lesson:
### 1. Close your open work honestly
List every open pull request with its true status: open, waiting for review from whom since when, changes requested, or merged. Give each one a next action and a name. 'Almost done' is not a status.

### 2. Write the reflection
Three short parts, in `docs/reflection.md`:
- **One thing you achieved, with evidence.** A link, a test, a screenshot, a merged pull request.
- **One thing that surprised you.** Something you believed in Week 1 that turned out to be wrong, and what replaced it.
- **One next goal, with a date.** Specific enough that someone could check on that date whether it happened.

### 3. Reread your first predictions
Open your first five predictions in this app and read them as if a stranger wrote them. Then paste them into Claude Code next to your reflection and ask where your thinking changed most. Keep what rings true. The reflection stays in your words.

### What this was for
Six weeks ago the goal was: build, test, and deploy a small app with Claude Code, and be able to explain what the AI wrote. You did that. The next goal is yours.

examples.caption: docs/reflection.md
examples.code:
## Open work
- PR #7 Blocked column: open, waiting for review from Naveen since 12 Dec. Next action: theirs.

## One thing I achieved
The suggest endpoint falls back to rules when the model is down. Evidence: test/assistant.test.js, and the demo with a wrong key.

## One thing that surprised me
I thought CI would catch bugs. It only catches the tests I wrote. The keyboard-only bug it could never see.

## Next goal
By 15 Dec: put the OpenAI API behind the same assistant function and compare the twenty-issue scores.

byHand.task: With Claude Code closed: list every open pull request with its true status, who it waits on, and the next action, in `docs/feature.md`. Then write `docs/reflection.md`: one thing you achieved with evidence, one thing that surprised you, and one next goal with a date. Reread your first five predictions in this app before you write.
checklist: Every open pull request has a true status and a name for the next action.
The reflection has one achievement with evidence, one surprise, and one dated goal.
I reread my first five predictions first.

withAI.task: Paste your first five predictions from this program into Claude Code next to your reflection and ask it where your thinking changed most. Keep what rings true. The reflection stays in your words.
withAI.prompt: Here are five predictions I wrote six weeks ago and my reflection today: [paste]. Where did my thinking change most, and where was I right for the wrong reason? Quote my words. Do not rewrite the reflection.
checklist: I compared my early predictions with what I can explain now.
The reflection is still in my words.

hints: If the achievement has no evidence, it is a feeling. Find the link.
A surprise is something you would have bet on and lost. Not 'I learned a lot'.
A goal with a day of the week on it gets done more often than one with a month.

glossary: Terminal
A text interface for running commands in a chosen folder.
Repository
A project's files and their recorded version history.
Commit
A recorded snapshot of changes in Git, stored on your machine until pushed.
Push
Sending your local commits to a remote such as GitHub.
Branch
A separate line of development in a repository, kept apart from main until reviewed.
Pull request
A request to review and merge a branch's changes into another branch.
Merge
Bringing one branch's commits into another, usually after review.
Dependency
A package of code that your project uses, listed in package.json.
Lockfile
package-lock.json: the exact versions that were installed, so every machine matches.
Environment variable
A named value given to a program at run time, such as PORT or an API key.
Secret
A value that must stay private: a key, token, or password. Never in code, prompts, or logs.
Frontend
The interface and behavior running in the user's browser.
Backend
The server-side program that handles requests and enforces the rules.
API
An agreed set of paths, methods, and shapes two programs use to talk.
Request and response
The browser sends a method, path, and optional body; the server replies with a status code and a body.
Status code
The number in a response that states the outcome: 200 ok, 201 created, 400 bad request, 404 not found, 500 server error.
Database
Where data is stored in tables so it can be searched and changed safely over time.
SQL
The language for talking to a database: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
Test
An automated check of one specific expected behavior. Green proves only what was written.
Refactor
Changing code structure without changing behavior. Tests stay green before and after.
CI
Continuous integration: checks that run automatically on a fresh machine when code changes.
CD
Continuous delivery or deployment: publishing a release after checks pass. A separate decision.
Deployment
Making a version of an application available where others can use it.
Container
A running instance of a Docker image: a packaged process with its own files and dependencies.
LLM
Large language model: a program that predicts likely next text from the text it is given.
Token
A fragment of text, roughly part of a word, that a model reads and writes one at a time.
Context window
Everything the model can take into account right now: your messages, files you include, and earlier turns.
Prompt
The instructions and context you give a model.
Hallucination
Fluent, plausible output that is not true. The reason you verify.
Agent
A model in a loop with tools: it reads, decides, acts, observes, and repeats. Claude Code is one.
Plan mode
Claude Code exploring and proposing without editing, so you can judge the approach first.
CLAUDE.md
Standing instructions Claude Code reads at the start of every session in a folder.
Skill
A folder with a SKILL.md describing a reusable procedure Claude Code loads when relevant or invoked.
Machine learning
Programs that learn a pattern from labelled examples and then predict or classify.
Generative AI
Machine learning models trained to produce new content such as text or code. An LLM is one.
Structured output
Asking the model API for a reply in a fixed shape, such as a JSON schema, so code can rely on it.
